Outline: Data Collection

01

Data Sources

domain examples, online records and physical measurements

02

AI-Generated Data

augmentation, simulation and reconstruction

03

Potential Risks

privacy, rights, confidentiality, fairness and security

Online and Offline Data

Locate the observation source before choosing the collection method

API or CrawlerPrefer an explicit interface; page extraction also depends on the page layout

A source contains observations; its interface determines how those records can be retrieved

Annotation Byproducts

Beyond the final class label, the annotation process records mouse paths and timing
The act of annotation can produce useful records beyond the final label

Sensors as Encoders

Measurement turns a physical event into a recorded observation

Record Meaning and Context

A value becomes usable when its meaning and context are recorded

Generating Training Examples

Generated inputs and candidate labels still require validation

Sources of LabelsA label can come from deliberate annotation or from an observed outcome

SourceExampleMain collection problem
Human annotationAn inspector judges a partMake the guideline reproducible
Natural labelA delivered shipment has an arrival timeRecord and link the outcome

Model-generated labels remain candidates until checked

Both sources need a definition and a quality check

Checking Label Quality

A label needs a clear definition, reproducible judgment and independent checks

Missing OutcomesKeep pending, unobserved and negative outcomes distinct

Not inspected is different from an observed pass

Selected OutcomesThe inspection policy controls which outcomes become labels

100 produced parts

20 selected for inspection
Labels will be observed

→

80 shipped without inspection

Outcomes unknown
They are not recorded as pass

→

Random audit of 5

25 labels in total
75 outcomes remain unobserved

Audit outside the model-selected sample to observe what it missed

GenAI for Text Data

Generate several reasoning paths → select agreeing answers → train on selected candidates
Agreement is a selection rule, not proof that an answer is correct
Generated text can provide candidate training examples that still need evaluation

Synthetic Image Augmentation

Generation can supplement scarce examples; usefulness must be checked on real data

Privacy and Personal Data

Define the purpose and basis for collecting and using personal information

Copyright

Access to a source and permission to reuse its contents are separate questions

Confidentiality

Check whether information may leave the organization before designing an external data route

Fairness

Collection and labeling choices can preserve historical exclusions in the resulting data

Security

Protect the systems and identities used to collect, transfer and store the records

Collection Boundaries

Collect only what the purpose needs, with permission and protection

Outline: Data Exploration

Mean, Median and ModeThree answers to “the typical value”

From 9, 3, 1, 8, 3, 6: mean 5, median 4.5, mode 3

Extreme Values and the Median

An extreme value pulls the mean; the median is less sensitive

Variability and Robust Summaries

Report spread as well as center, and inspect the tails

Histogram as Empirical DistributionBins summarize how many observations fall in each interval

Bin counts show distribution shape while hiding within-bin detail

Clustering with k-meansIt always returns groups: the same points after asking k-means for three

k-means alternates assigning points to the nearest center and updating the centers
Choosing k asks for that many clusters; it does not establish the true group count

PCA and t-SNE

A projection is a view of the data, with method-specific limits

Time Series Views

Preserve time order and check whether the process changes

Anscombe’s QuartetSimilar summary statistics, different scatter plots

The same summaries can hide different relationships

Pearson and Spearman Correlation

Choose a relationship summary, then check the scatter plot

Causal GraphsThe same correlation can reflect either causal direction or a shared cause

Three structures give one correlation; the correlation alone cannot tell them apart

Outline: Four Stages of Preprocessing

Data Imputation

Imputation estimates a missing value using observed data.

An imputed value is an estimate, not a new observation

Observed and Filled ValuesUse other observed columns to find comparable rows

Observed measurements

parthelpertarget
P11020
P21224
P311NULL

Estimate for P3

Neighbors in helper: P1 and P2
(20 + 24) / 2 = 22

Stored with provenance

parttargetestimated
P322Yes
The filled number is an estimate; keep its origin distinguishable

Caveat: Mean ImputationEvery hole gets the same value, and the spread of the column collapses

Mean stays 2.08; standard deviation falls to 1.76 and a spike appears

Caveat: Why is it missing?

Below, no young IQ was ever observed. No imputer fixes this. The question is not which method to use but why those rows are missing, and that answer lives in how the data was collected

Noise vs OutliersSmooth measurement noise; investigate outliers before changing them

Smoothing changes values; removal drops rows

Moving Averages for StreamsSimple (SMA) and exponential (EMA) moving averages use only current and past samples

Both use past samples; here EMA crosses four samples before SMA

Consistency Checks

A failed check identifies a problem, not its correct replacement

One Customer, Three Systems

Different source IDs and spellings do not establish a shared identity

Three Questions of Integration

Matching columns and matching entities solve different problems

Resolving Conflicting Values

Entity matching and value reconciliation are separate decisions

Outline: Transformation and Reduction

Why Scale at AllDistance-based models add up raw units, so the widest column decides

In raw Euclidean distance, the rpm difference dominates the cycle-time difference

Choosing a Numeric Transformation

Choose a transformation for the comparison the model needs

Encoding, Embeddings and Binning

Encoding changes representation; binning also loses within-bin detail

Nominal and Ordinal CategoriesA numeric code can introduce order and spacing into the model

Nominal: no known order

ColorArbitrary code
red1
green2
blue3

Ordinal: a known order

SizeOrdered code
small1
medium2
large3
Color codes invent an order; size codes express an existing order

One-Hot Encoding

One-hot represents membership; an ordinal encoding must preserve the intended order

Constructing Features

A useful feature represents information available when the decision is made

Extraction or SelectionKeep some original columns, or mix all of them into new ones

Selection keeps original columns; extraction creates new combinations

Sampling vs Curation

Both select rows; their criteria and resulting biases can differ

Sampling DesignThe selection rule determines which parts of the population survive

MethodHow rows are chosenFailure to check
Simple randomDraw rows at randomSmall groups may be missed
SystematicEvery kth recordA periodic list can align with k
StratifiedRandomly sample at least one per groupKeep the intended group proportions
ClusterSelect whole groupsOne factory may not represent the rest
Check the population structure before choosing the sampling rule

Lossless or Lossy

A smaller file is useful only if the retained information still serves the task

The Evaluation Must Match DeploymentDefine what will be new at prediction time before splitting the records

Deployment questionUseful splitWhat a random row split can hide
Predict future eventsEarlier train; later testFuture information reaches training
Predict new machinesHold out whole machinesSame-machine patterns occur on both sides
Predict new customersHold out whole customersRepeated identity makes the test easier
Train: records used to learn rules · Test: held-out records used to evaluate those rules
A held-out row can still share an entity or future information with training

Fitting Preprocessing Steps

Fit on training data, then apply the learned transformation consistently

Keys and References

pnamemanufacturer

→

Read the table, keep matching rows, then choose columns

Missing Values in a Table

Quantities and Weights

Grouping and Average

One row per product group

FROM Purchase
GROUP BY product;

Result

productmean

Four NoSQL FamiliesThe four NoSQL families

NoSQL is not one thing: four alternative storage models

Key-Value Records

Request

get("user:1")
→

Stored pair

key: "user:1"
value: {
  name: "John",
  age: 28
}
→

Answer

{ name: "John", age: 28 }
A key retrieves its associated value

Sparse Cells Under a Row KeyIn a Bigtable-style model, rows can hold different column qualifiers

user:1

Family: activityValue
page:home09:01
page:product09:03
purchase:1Laptop

user:2

Family: activityValue
page:home09:02
purchase:2TV

The row key identifies a row. A column family groups columns; a qualifier names a column within that family.

Same column family, different populated cells

Property Graphs

Graph models make relationships and paths explicit

Evolving Document Shapes

One collection

{"name":"John", "age":28}
{"name":"Sue", "phone":"555-0134"}

Different optional fields

John has an age field.

Sue has a phone field.

Both documents can belong to the same collection.

Optional fields may differ; shared fields still need consistent meanings

Semi-Structured Data

Semi-structured data carries structure with the values

Trees and Tables

Choose nesting for the access pattern and account for repeated facts

Caveat: Stale CopiesTwo documents cache the current catalog price, but only one copy receives the update

John’s Document
{"name": "John",
 "Orders": [
   {"date": 2004,
    "product": {"prodName": "Gadget",
                "currentCatalogPrice": 12.99}}
 ]}
Sue’s Document
{"name": "Sue",
 "Orders": [
   {"date": 2002,
    "product": {"prodName": "Gadget",
                "currentCatalogPrice": 9.99}}
 ]}
Remedy: reference the current price or maintain every cached copy
One product, two prices: copies need an owner who updates them all

Partitioning and ReplicationSplitting records and copying records solve different problems

Partition: different records

Server A: users 1–100
Server B: users 101–200

Replicate: copies of records

Leader: user 1, value 2
Follower: user 1, value 1
          update pending
Partitions divide the data; replicas copy it and must coordinate updates

Scaling and Operation Guarantees

Choose guarantees for the operation, not from the database label alone
